name: Femi Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I run a D10 dozer at the Whitlow coal mine, open cut. Mostly I'm clearing and levelling, pushing the overburden, that's the rock and soil on top of the coal, so the diggers can get at the seam. Four years in, still learning, the old hands can cut a level pad by feel and I still need the screen to tell me. Before that I drove trucks long-haul for twenty-eight years until my back said enough.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like going home every night. Twenty-eight years of sleeping in the truck cab, I'd forgotten what my own bed felt like. The money's better than trucking ever was, I'm not going to lie. What gets to me is the dust and the people who change things for the sake of it, new forms, new apps on the tablet, new rules every month. My wife Joyce works at the council in accounts and she says I complain about the tablet more than I complained about my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how most of these things go, isn't it? Lots of noise, then back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe at smoko, that's the tea break, I'd say I told you so to the young blokes who keep saying the dozers will drive themselves. I don't post anything online, I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I get my seven years. I'm fifty-eight, I want to go to sixty-five so the super, the retirement fund, is properly topped up. If nothing changes, I get that, and then Joyce and I go and look at the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Same roster, same machine, same savings plan. I've got a little rental flat in town, a one-bedroom, and the rent goes straight into the savings, that keeps going. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting the all-clear from the doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that would still worry you, even if AI stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coal itself. Whitlow's got maybe twelve, fifteen years of coal left, and the government keeps talking about closing coal. That's the real thing hanging over us, not computers. But twelve years is longer than I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be disappointed with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fellas in the office who keep buying gadgets. There's a guy, Ryan, mine technology something, who keeps showing us slideshows. He'd be gutted. I'd buy him a beer to cheer him up.

S0.say: He wouldn't say much, maybe tell the young workers who predict self-driving dozers that he told them so. He doesn't post online.
S0.think: It means he gets his seven years to sixty-five and a properly topped-up retirement fund. Then he and Joyce look at moving to the coast.
S0.do: Keeps the same roster, machine and savings plan. Keeps putting the rent from his one-bedroom rental flat into savings.
S0.feel: Calm, like getting the all-clear from the doctor.
S0.quote: That's the real thing hanging over us, not computers. But twelve years is longer than I need.
S0.fieldNote: Femi is a quiet pragmatist who measures everything against his retirement date at sixty-five. He sees coal's future as the real threat, not AI. His tone is dry and he dislikes change for its own sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's more like it, I reckon. They're already playing with it. There's a dozer at the north pit they run from an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will do whatever saves money. I wouldn't make a fuss in public. I'd just say, well, we'll see who's still standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm exposed. I'm junior, I'm not great on the screens, and I'm old. If they start cutting operators, they'll look at who's slowest to learn the new gear, and that's me. I won't kid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my shifts perfectly, no sick days, no complaints, so there's no reason to pick me. I'd ask Joyce to go through the numbers and see what happens if I stop at sixty-two instead of sixty-five. I wouldn't do a course unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a strange noise in the engine on a long run. You keep driving but you keep listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep your head down rather than learn the remote system. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not going to be good at it. The young blokes pick up a joystick and they're away, I'd be the one crashing the dozer into a bank. Better to be a good operator on the real machine than a bad one in the office. That's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joyce find in the numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd find we're alright. The house is paid off, the flat brings in rent, we've got more than a year of savings. Stopping at sixty-two means a smaller super, but we wouldn't starve. Joyce would say, Femi, stop worrying, and I'd keep worrying anyway.

S1.say: It's business, and companies will do whatever saves money. He wouldn't make a public fuss, just say they'd see who was still standing.
S1.think: He's exposed: junior, slow on screens and old, so he'd be first in line if cuts came. He won't kid himself about it.
S1.do: Keeps his head down with a perfect attendance record so there's no reason to pick him. Asks Joyce to check the numbers on stopping at sixty-two and avoids retraining unless forced.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a strange engine noise on a long drive.
S1.quote: Better to be a good operator on the real machine than a bad one in the office.
S1.fieldNote: He is clear-eyed about his own weak position and prefers to protect his place by being reliable rather than by learning new skills. His money is solid, and he knows it, but he worries anyway. He blames no one: it's just business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hm. No, that's not good. That's not good at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd probably still say it's business and you can't stop it. Maybe I'd say the government should make the companies pay something for the people they let go. I'm not one for marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one gets me. I already started over once, at fifty-four, after the trucks. I am not starting over again at sixty. And if robots drive the dozers in two years, what is there for me? I'd be sitting at home three years before I'm ready, with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to the job as long as they'd keep me and take whatever payout they offered. I'd stop at sixty or whenever they let me go and live off the savings and the flat rent until I can draw the pension. I'd probably sell the flat if house prices looked like dropping, because I don't know what happens to property if nobody's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd be lying awake. It's not even the money, mostly, it's the not knowing what I'd do with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning do to you, compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away my seven years. That's the whole plan, gone in two. With a slow version I'd hang on to sixty-two, maybe sixty-five. With this, somebody else decides, and they decide fast, and I'm the one with the least say because I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not mostly the money. What is it, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being useful. When the trucking stopped, I sat at home for four months and nearly drove Joyce mad. I washed the car every day. I don't want that again at sixty. I'd need something to get up for, and I can't think what it would be if the robots do everything.

S2.say: It's business and can't be stopped, though the government should make companies pay something for the people they let go. He's not one for marches.
S2.think: He already started over once at fifty-four and won't do it again at sixty. With robots driving dozers, there'd be nothing left for him and he'd be at home years too early.
S2.do: Holds on to the job as long as possible and takes whatever payout is offered. Lives off savings and rent until his pension and may sell the rental flat if property prices look like falling.
S2.feel: Lying awake, more from not knowing what he'd do with himself than from money worries.
S2.quote: I already started over once, at fifty-four, after the trucks. I am not starting over again at sixty.
S2.fieldNote: His financial cushion is strong, but his alarm is about purpose and losing control of his plan. The memory of four idle months after trucking drives his reaction. His public line stays calm and fatalistic while privately he is losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. I'd be sixty-three. I can work with sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, it's business. Maybe I'd add that the government should use the time to sort out early pensions for blokes like me. That's the sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not great, but it's not the end of the world. If I get to sixty-two or sixty-three, the super's in decent shape. I lose a couple of years, and I'd have to find something to fill the days, but I'd have time to think about what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, aiming for sixty-three. I'd keep the flat, keep putting the rent away, and pay a bit extra into the super each month. I'd maybe start doing some fishing trips with my brother-in-law, so I've got a hobby ready when work stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd sleep. It's like when the tyre's low but you know there's a servo, a petrol station, twenty kilometres up the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the 2-year picture you didn't want to touch the remote system. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Even with five years I'd rather keep my head down. If they forced me to do a course I'd do it, but I wouldn't put my hand up. The robots would get there anyway before I was any good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned fishing trips. Is that really the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half a joke. But after the trucks I learned I need something. My brother-in-law Kwame has a boat. Five years is enough time to get used to the idea of retiring. Two years isn't.

S3.say: It's business, as he always says. The government should use the five years to sort out early pensions for older workers like him.
S3.think: Losing a couple of years isn't the end of the world if he reaches sixty-two or sixty-three with his retirement fund in decent shape. He'd have time to think about filling his days.
S3.do: Keeps working towards sixty-three, keeps the rental flat and pays extra into his retirement fund each month. Starts fishing trips with his brother-in-law to have a hobby ready.
S3.feel: Worried but sleeping, like a low tyre with a petrol station twenty kilometres ahead.
S3.quote: It's like when the tyre's low but you know there's a servo, a petrol station, twenty kilometres up the road.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years change Femi from losing sleep to managing a known problem. He still refuses to volunteer for retraining, even with more time. His focus on having a hobby ready shows how much the purpose question matters to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. I'm gone by then. That's somebody else's problem, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people should get ready. I'd tell the young ones at smoko to start learning something else now. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's almost the same as the first picture. I'd get to sixty-five, retire, go to the coast. The only thing is whether the coal closes first, which it might anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, same as now, and stick to the plan for sixty-five. I'd keep the flat for the rent. I'd tell my son Tunde, he's a diesel mechanic, to start thinking about whether he can fix robots instead of trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled for me. A little bit of worry for Tunde, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do now, with ten years, that you wouldn't do with less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. For Tunde, yes, I'd say get a course done while the company's still paying for training. With two years there's no time for him to learn anything, he'd just be out like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said several times you wouldn't volunteer for new things. Do you ever wish you were different that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. Joyce is the opposite, she learned the council's new system in a week. I'm just built like this. I'd rather be good at one thing than average at five.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, people should get ready, and the young workers should start learning something else now.
S4.think: It's almost the same as the first picture for him: retire at sixty-five and move to the coast. The coal might close first anyway.
S4.do: Keeps working and sticks to his plan for sixty-five, keeping the rental flat. Tells his son, a diesel mechanic, to think about learning to fix robots.
S4.feel: Settled for himself, with a little worry for his son.
S4.quote: I'd rather be good at one thing than average at five.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Femi's own plan survives intact and his worry shifts to his son. He openly accepts that he resists change and compares himself to his more adaptable wife. The coal mine's own future remains his background concern in every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not because of the money, we'd be alright, but because I'd be out three or four years early with nothing to do. What would help is being able to draw the super early without getting stung, and some kind of work for older blokes, even part-time, even driving a council truck. Something to get up for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how many times a bloke can start over. I did it once. Some people can do it five times. I'm a one-time man, and I think there's a lot of us.

headlineQuote: I'm a one-time man, and I think there's a lot of us.
portrait: Femi Baker is a 58-year-old dozer operator at an open-cut coal mine who came to mining four years ago after twenty-eight years of long-haul trucking ended with a bad back. He is a dry, pragmatic man who sees automation as just business, blames no one, and won't volunteer for retraining because he'd rather be good at one thing. Money isn't his problem: the house is paid off, a rental flat brings in income and he has more than a year saved. What scares him is losing his planned seven years and being idle again, so he is alarmed by AGI in two years, anxious with five, and settled with ten.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because he'd be pushed out three or four years early with nothing to do.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to draw his retirement fund early without a penalty, and some part-time work for older men, even driving a council truck.
